title: Impact Manifest
description: An Impact Manifest is a machine-readable safety assertion about a proposed infrastructure mutation. A `terraform show -json` plan says WHAT will change; an Impact Manifest says whether the change is SAFE, and — critically — records what it could NOT determine. It is produced by consuming a plan plus (optionally) live cloud state, and is designed to be generated by any tool, for any provider. The governing rule of the whole format: a verdict of 'safe' is a positive claim that must be earned with evidence; the absence of a known problem is 'unknown', never 'safe'.

schema_version.description: Version of THIS format the document conforms to (semver). This IS the spec version. Compatibility is keyed off the MAJOR component: a consumer MUST refuse a major version it does not implement rather than risk misreading, and within a major it recognizes MUST ignore fields it does not know (which, for non-standard data, live under `extensions`). See the specification's Compatibility section.

assertion_id.description: Opaque unique id for this assertion, so it can be referenced from logs, PR comments, and audit trails.

generated_at.description: When the assertion was produced. Safety verdicts about live state decay — a consumer may reject an assertion that is too old to trust.

valid_until.description: The moment after which this manifest MUST NOT be relied on for a gate decision. A 'safe' verdict is only true as of the state it was computed against, and state drifts — often fast. A consumer that receives an expired manifest MUST NOT treat it as authoritative; it MUST re-compute. Absent means the producer stated no window, and a strict consumer SHOULD supply its own maximum age.

state_observed_at.description: The timestamp of the FRESHEST live-state observation the verdicts rest on (which may be earlier than `generated_at`). Lets a consumer judge staleness against reality, not just against when the document was written.

producer.description: The tool that produced this document AND what it was able to see. Provenance matters: two tools may disagree about the same change, and a reader must know which one spoke, what it queried, and what access it held — an unknown is only interpretable if you know whether the producer even had live access.

integrity.description: Optional detached-signature slot so a manifest can be attested and tamper-evidence established. A manifest without integrity is usable but NOT attestable; a consumer that requires attestation MUST reject an unsigned manifest. v0.1 defines the slot and a canonicalization rule but does not mandate a signing scheme — see the specification's Integrity section for the layering plan (in-toto/DSSE, Sigstore).

source.description: The artifact this assertion was derived from (a Terraform plan today; the field is structured so other change sources can be added without breaking readers).

evidence.description: The shared pool of evidence actually gathered to reach the verdicts below. Every verdict points into this pool by id. This is the auditable answer to 'how do you know?' — a verdict with no evidence is an opinion, and a reader can see that.

changes.description: One entry per resource change in the plan that this assertion covers. A plan is a set of changes applied atomically, so the safe/unsafe decision is made over the whole set, but each change is assessed on its own so a reader can see exactly which one is dangerous.

verdict.description: The single roll-up decision a CI gate acts on. It is a pure function of the per-change assessments and the applied policy; it exists so a machine does not have to re-derive intent from the details.

extensions.description: The ONLY place non-standard, producer- or consumer-specific fields may appear. Every core object in this schema is strict (additionalProperties:false) so a producer bug surfaces immediately during validation; anything outside the standard goes here instead. A consumer MUST ignore extension keys it does not recognize — that is what makes forward-compatible additions possible without breaking older readers.

confidence.description: How much the tool trusts the VALUE it just gave — orthogonal to the value itself. A verdict of 'value: none' with 'confidence: low' means 'I found no impact but I am not sure I looked everywhere', which a strict policy should treat differently from 'value: none, confidence: high'. Note that 'unknown' is a VALUE (I could not determine), not a confidence level (I determined it, but weakly).

evidenceRefs.description: Ids of entries in the top-level `evidence` pool that support the verdict this appears on.

id.description: Referenced by verdicts via their `evidence` arrays.

source.description: Where this fact came from. The distinction is the point: 'terraform_plan' is what the plan asserts (and the plan trusts state, which may be wrong); 'live_state' is what was observed by querying the provider directly; 'heuristic' is a rule of thumb, not a measurement. A reader weighs these differently.

query.description: What was actually asked to obtain this fact — a plan JSON pointer, an API/CLI call, a policy rule name. Makes the verdict reproducible.

observation.description: What came back. The raw finding, in human-readable form.

observed_at.description: When the observation was made. Live-state facts have a shelf life.

provider.description: The cloud/provider the fact pertains to, when relevant (e.g. a provider address). Optional and provider-agnostic.

name.description: Name of the tool that produced the document.

access.description: What the producer was able to see when it ran. An 'unknown' verdict is only interpretable if you know whether the producer even had the access to determine otherwise — a delete assessed by a tool with no live-state access is unknown for a very different reason than one assessed by a fully-credentialed tool.

live_state.description: 'queried' = the producer reached the provider and read live state. 'unavailable' = it tried and could not (no credentials, network). 'not_attempted' = it ran plan-only by choice. The difference explains why unknowns exist.

scope.description: Human description of the identity/permissions the producer held (e.g. 'read-only, Reader on subscription abc-123'). Bounds what it could have known — a reader can see that a narrow role explains a narrow assessment.

integrity.description: Detached integrity and signing metadata. The signature covers the CANONICAL form of the manifest with this `integrity` object removed (a signature cannot sign itself). Canonicalization is JCS — JSON Canonicalization Scheme, RFC 8785 — which fixes key ordering, whitespace, and number formatting so two conformant producers serializing the same logical document produce byte-identical input to the hash. A verifier reconstructs the signed payload by deleting `integrity`, applying JCS, and checking against `digest`/`signature`. v0.1 fixes this canonicalization rule and the slot; it does not yet mandate a single signing scheme.

digest.description: Digest of the canonicalized payload (this `integrity` object removed). Lets a consumer detect tampering even before verifying a signature.

signature.description: A detached signature over the digested payload.

key_id.description: Identifier of the signing key, for verifier key lookup.

certificate.description: Optional PEM certificate or a reference to one (e.g. a Sigstore identity).

envelope.description: Optional pointer to a full attestation carrying this manifest as its subject, for teams already running an attestation framework.

type.description: The attestation format wrapping this manifest.

reference.description: URI or storage reference to the envelope.

type.description: The kind of change artifact consumed. An enum (not a free string) so a consumer can refuse a source it has no rules for. Additional sources are added by extending this enum in a future schema_version.

tool_version.description: Version of the change tool that produced the source artifact (e.g. the Terraform version). Behaviour of the plan format varies by version.

format_version.description: Version of the source artifact's own format (e.g. Terraform's plan JSON `format_version`).

reference.description: An identifier for the specific artifact consumed — a filename, a content hash, a pipeline run id. Lets an audit tie the assertion back to the exact plan it judged.

rationale.description: A human-readable reason for the value. REQUIRED on every verdict, including 'unknown' — a bare 'unknown' with no reason is a bug, not an answer. This is what a reviewer reads when deciding whether to override the machine.

value.description: Whether applying the change interrupts something currently serving. 'none' = verified not to interrupt anything live. 'at_risk' = it may, depending on conditions the tool could not fully resolve. 'interrupts' = it will take a live thing offline. 'unknown' = the tool could not determine whether anything live depends on the target. 'none' and 'unknown' are deliberately distinct: the first is a finding, the second is the absence of one.

serves_production_traffic.description: Whether the affected resource is currently serving production traffic, as best the tool could establish by querying live state. The plan cannot know this; it is the enrichment the format exists to carry.

expected_interruption.description: Human description of the interruption if any — what goes down, and for how long.

value.description: Whether the change can be undone. 'reversible' = fully, with no loss. 'reversible_with_data_loss' = the resource can be recreated but data written since is gone. 'irreversible' = there is no mechanism to get back to the prior state. 'unknown' = the tool could not establish a reversal path — which must be treated as at least as dangerous as irreversible, never as reversible.

mechanism.description: HOW the change would be reversed, concretely (e.g. 'restore from snapshot X', 're-apply the prior Terraform state'). A reversibility claim with no mechanism is not credible.

window.description: The time window in which reversal is possible before it stops being possible (e.g. 'until the resource is destroyed', 'within the 7-day soft-delete retention'). Reversibility often has an expiry.

cost.description: The OPERATIONAL cost of reversing — not whether it is possible, but what it costs. 'Reversible by restoring a snapshot taken 14 hours ago' is technically reversible and operationally a disaster: up to 14 hours of writes lost. Record the data-loss window and disruption here. If reversing loses data, `value` MUST be 'reversible_with_data_loss', not 'reversible', and this field quantifies the loss.

value.description: What happens to data. 'no_data_loss' = no data is affected. 'recoverable_loss' = data is removed but a recovery path exists (a backup, a snapshot). 'unrecoverable_loss' = data becomes permanently unrecoverable. 'unknown' = the tool could not establish whether recoverable copies exist — treated as unrecoverable for safety, not as safe.

at_risk.description: What specifically becomes unrecoverable (or would, absent the recovery path named in the rationale).

value.description: Direction of the change's effect on security posture. 'widened' = exposure increases, an identity is weakened, or an audit/logging control is broken. 'improved' = the opposite. 'unchanged' = verified no net effect. 'unknown' = could not determine — not to be read as 'unchanged'.

concerns.description: Specific posture changes found, each classed by kind so a policy can weight them.

kind.description: 'exposure' = network/public reachability widens; 'identity' = an authn/authz control weakens; 'audit' = a logging/monitoring/immutability control is removed or degraded.

detail.description: Human description of the specific concern.

direction.description: Direction of the change's effect on spend. Cost is a safety dimension too — a change that silently 100x's a bill is a production incident of a different kind.

recurrence.description: Whether the cost effect is a one-time charge or an ongoing rate change. A recurring increase compounds; a one-time charge does not.

estimate.description: Optional magnitude. Absent when the tool can state direction but not amount.

amount.description: Estimated magnitude of the change, in `currency`.

stateConfidence.description: How much the tool trusts that the recorded state the plan was computed against still matches reality. This dimension exists because a plan TRUSTS state, and state drifts: a plan can confidently describe a change to a resource whose real shape no longer matches what Terraform recorded. When state is not trustworthy, no downstream verdict about that resource can be trusted either.

value.description: 'state_matches_reality' = live state was queried and agrees with recorded state. 'drift_detected' = live state was queried and DISAGREES (the plan is reasoning about a resource that no longer looks like this). 'state_stale' = recorded state is old enough or the resource volatile enough that it cannot be trusted. 'not_verified' = the tool did not check live state (distinct from checking and finding a match). 'unknown' = the tool tried to check and could not.

verified_against_live.description: True only when the tool actually queried the provider to compare. 'not_verified' with this false is honest; a match claim with this false is not.

precondition.description: An assertion that must hold for apply to be safe. Preconditions turn 'this is dangerous' into 'this is safe IF …', which is what actually unblocks a change: satisfy the precondition and re-run.

id.description: Stable id for the precondition, so a re-run can report the same one as now satisfied.

description.description: Human statement of what must be true (e.g. 'a snapshot of the disk exists that is newer than the last write').

check.description: Machine-checkable form of the assertion, when one exists — a query or expression a tool can evaluate to satisfied/unsatisfied.

status.description: 'satisfied' = verified true. 'unsatisfied' = verified false (this is what blocks). 'unknown' = could not verify — blocks under a strict policy, because an unverified precondition is not a met one.

rationale.description: Why the status is what it is.

address.description: The change tool's address for the resource (e.g. a Terraform resource address). The stable key a reader uses to find this exact change in the original plan.

resource_type.description: Provider resource type, verbatim from the plan (e.g. an azurerm/aws/google type). The format does not enumerate types — it is provider-agnostic.

name.description: The resource's local name within its module.

provider.description: Provider address the resource belongs to. Optional; provider-agnostic.

actions.description: The action(s) the plan takes on this resource, using the change tool's own vocabulary (Terraform: no-op | create | read | update | delete; a replace is the pair delete+create). Carried verbatim so the assertion cannot silently disagree with the plan about what is happening.

severity.description: The per-change roll-up a reader scans first. 'blocking' = at least one dimension says this is dangerous. 'unknown' = at least one safety-critical dimension could not be determined, so this change cannot be certified safe. 'unknown' NEVER collapses to 'informational' — that collapse is the exact failure this format exists to prevent.

rationale.description: One-line human summary of why this change has the severity it does.

decision.description: The whole-plan decision. 'safe' is a POSITIVE claim: every change was assessed and none is dangerous and nothing safety-critical is unknown. 'caution' = proceed with a human in the loop. 'blocked' = at least one change is dangerous under policy. 'unknown' = something safety-critical could not be determined; the plan is NOT safe, it is unproven. A conformant consumer must never map 'unknown' to 'safe'.

rationale.description: Human explanation of the decision, naming the change(s) that drove it.

blocking_changes.description: Addresses of the changes responsible for a 'blocked' or 'unknown' decision, so a gate can report them without re-deriving.

unknowns_present.description: True if any dimension anywhere in the document is 'unknown'. A loud, top-level flag so an unknown can never hide in the details and be skimmed past as safe.

policy.description: The policy applied to turn per-change assessments into this decision, when one was applied (e.g. by a CI gate). Absent when the document only describes and does not judge.
